extracted.intended_audience: British Parliamentarians, policymakers, and officials overseeing the East India Company and colonial revenue administration
extracted.subtask_description: A parliamentary speech setting standards for how ministers should manage conquered Indian territories' revenues, debt, and reconstruction — arguing principles for just and effective colonial administration and fiscal policy. Focused on the Carnatic and Tanjore cases but articulating general governance rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize restoration over immediate extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Government must begin by maintaining the people; economic recovery requires public expense first — 'the road to economy lies not through receipt, but through expense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After long periods of vexation and plunder, people need support (provision of habitation, seed, stock, capital) before they can be taxed. Ministers should reduce non-essential establishments and employ every shilling derived from producing parts to reanimate unproductive parts; otherwise taxation on relics is tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not levy public charges on the devastated remains
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to compute and charge for public service upon the relics of a country devastated by war and misgovernment — likened to 'tyranny sublimed into madness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charging a ruined country for public services or using its wrecked state as a basis to fund obligations to private claimants is immoral and politically insane; ministers must not rest revenue calculations on such wreckage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure basic inputs for population and cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recovery of population and cultivation requires prior provision of habitation, seed, stock, and capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People 'propagate... by the mouth' — oppression, extortion, and usury prevent family formation and agricultural recovery. Policy should provide these essentials rather than expect immediate returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in and maintain critical irrigation infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reservoirs and waterworks are the 'national bank' of the Carnatic and must be maintained or the country perishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Carnatic lacks perennial streams and depends on many reservoirs (hundreds to thousands); these are costly to build and maintain but indispensable. Restoration policy should prioritize repairing reservoirs and watercourses before expecting revenue revival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base revenue estimates on recent, authorized, factual reports not nostalgic speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use up-to-date committee reports and actual transactions rather than speculative 'peace' estimates from better times (e.g., Macartney's 1781 peace estimate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Macartney's 1781 figures were speculative and reflected former prosperity; the committee at Madras and recent leases gave concrete net receipts (e.g., ~480,000 l. in 1782). Ministers should not suppress or prefer speculative numbers over recorded, recent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and production of relevant records
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers must produce and not suppress reports, correspondence, and committee findings bearing on revenue and management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressing decisive papers (e.g., the Madras committee report) or ignoring records corrupts policy debate; full disclosure is necessary for honest decisions and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not restore mismanagement without protections and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Territories should not be returned to their former mismanaging rulers 'without condition, without arrangement, without stipulation' that protect natives and preserve improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivering lands back to the Nabob without safeguards risks ruin for tenants, farmers, and British appointees; any restoration must include stipulations for protection of cultivators and revenue tenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize standing defence and civil governance over private creditor claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Public funds must secure army, civil establishment, and government functioning before satisfying private debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting preference to private claims robs the public in army pay, administration, credit, and investment — undermines security and long-term revenue; priority should be public defence and administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert war devastation into enforceable debts on the population
rubrics_metrics.description: Calamities of war should not be metamorphosed into debts charged upon the future production of the people who suffered them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating losses from invasion as arrears or debts to be repaid by the devastated populace perpetuates ruin; in leases and accounting, invasion normally releases rent rather than creates a debt to be collected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid enabling private usury and high-interest assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not permit soucars/assignees to mortgage revenues and charge exorbitant interest (24–48% compounded), profiteering from territorial revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Company needs repayment, it should accept assignments directly or lend at reasonable market rates (e.g., 8%) rather than allowing intermediaries to extract ruinous usury and foster collusion with Company servants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent conflicts of interest where creditors are their own security
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers must not authorize arrangements where creditors become 'soucar security' for their own claims, effectively granting themselves additional interest and security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving creditors the power to secure revenues for repayment of their own extortions compounds injustice — the House should scrutinize who benefits from security provisions and forbid self-dealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide meaningful, funded protection and compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises of protection and compensation to dispossessed or endangered persons are empty unless backed by defined powers and funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering 'protection and compensation' without a source of power or fund is mockery; any remedial scheme must specify from what authority and budget it will be executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perpetual confiscation as punishment for future wars
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties that confiscate revenues indefinitely to cover possible future debts (e.g., if Company provokes war) are unjust and effectively permanent dispossession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscation tied to uncertain future Company debts should not be framed as temporary; in practice it becomes permanent subjection and revenue loss for the subject state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat a company's own lost receipts as an external debt owed by the territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Company cannot legitimately claim the Carnatic 'owes' it money when the revenues in question are the Company's own estate — 'to say they are in debt to themselves is only talking nonsense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounting must distinguish between private/public external claims and revenue shortfalls caused by war or mismanagement of the Company's own holdings; improper accounting turns the Company's losses into burdens on natives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize and reject fictitious or inflated private debt claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Many private claims and supposed debts are fictitious, inflated, or the product of extortion and should not be preferred over real public needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers and the House must examine the nature and validity of private claims; precedence of such claims often masks usury and collusion and undermines public finances.
